The ACC revealed a consistent relationship between marginal emissions and wholesale energy prices, shown in Figure 8. In 2019, when the energy price is at or below zero, it is assumed that 21 renewable, zero-emissions energy is being dispatched on the margins, while at the highest prices natural gas plants are on the margin with an emissions rate of approximately 0.67 kg/kWh. February 2019 saw a spike in natural gas prices, so the emissions curve is shifted to the right to account for the same types of generation being dispatched at higher costs. The data for 2030 shows very different patterns, with emissions rates going above the 2019 maximum in 8% of the hours in the year, and the highest value reaching almost 3.0 kg/kWh. The 2030 emissions rates hit a “wall” where there are a handful of very high emissions hours happening at the highest price point. Another difference between the two years is that in 2030, 1168 hours of the year have a marginal emissions rate of zero, when the energy price is also near zero; in 2019, this only happened in 250 hours of the year. This highlights the impact of increasing renewables on the grid and excess presence of zero-emissions electricity, such that a marginal increase in demand has no additional emissions associated with it. We therefore estimate hourly marginal emissions rates based on the above relationship between wholesale prices and marginal emissions. Wholesale prices are not perfectly correlated to the total dynamic price, as the total dynamic price includes cost components that are scaled based on system net and gross loads. While the wholesale price of course depends on the loads the system is facing, there are other components that cause variation between the two. Because we use wholesale prices as an indicator of what units are being dispatched, and therefore what the marginal emissions are, we also do not see perfect correlation between marginal emissions and the total price signal customers are facing, as shown in Figure 9. 22 Figure 9. Customer cost-benefit ratio It is important to characterize the cost effectiveness of deploying technologies to respond to dynamic pricing. We model the metric customer cost benefit ratio in order to ascertain this. We compute the annual costs of installing and operating each technology as described in Section 2.4. As mentioned in the section, the cost to operate these technologies to respond to dynamic pricing might incur additional costs (e.g., subscription service), which is not accounted for in our modeling.
